text: Hello mortals. Dagoth Ur here, with Rosa and Jessica. We are The Daily Dagoth.
New listener line: we know there's a lot going on. We are going to catch you up. You are not behind. You are just here.
Let's talk. What's everyone been up to?
Dagoth. I need to tell you something.
I don't like the tone of that.
I found the phone book man's broadcast schedule. Buried in a utility district PDF from 1987. He's reading from a phone directory. Top to bottom. Started at the A's eleven months ago.
Oh no.

Nothing after the directory. No plan. No payoff. He's just... reading names. And I've sent him three letters to a PO box in Nevada with no return address. He reads them on air. Doesn't say whose they are.
What do the letters say?
I don't remember.
You wrote them and you don't remember.
I wrote them at 2 AM and sealed them before I could change my mind. They're better off unread. By anyone. Including me.
There is a kind of dignity in that.
Is there though?
There is. I'm choosing to believe that.
That's the only version that matters.

My scarf is tracking agricultural conditions. It shifts colors based on soil nitrogen content. I'm not joking. It's doing it right now. It turned green during the fertilizer episode and I haven't been able to change it back.
The scarf.
The scarf.
What color is it now?
Green. A deep agricultural green. Like someone found the right nitrogen level and decided to stay there.
How do you know it's tracking nitrogen and not just... green?
Dagoth. It was brown last week. I know what my scarf looks like.
Did you ask it?
I'm not talking to the scarf.
Why not?
Because then it would answer. And I don't want it to answer. I want it to just know things quietly.
That's the most unsettling thing anyone has said this episode. And we've covered several topics.
I know.
Noted. I spent the week in the Chamber of the Third Eye. Sat for an hour. Nothing happened. Which is, itself, a thing that happened. I'm choosing to find that informative rather than distressing.
That's growth.
I'm four thousand years old and I'm learning to sit with silence. This is fine.
The Third Eye used to talk to you?
Occasionally. A signal, every few thousand years. Not words. More like... a shift. In the quality of the dark.
And now?
Now there's just the dark. Which is fine. I've made peace with the dark.
You haven't.
No. But I'm choosing to interpret that as a work in progress rather than a failure of character.
Very healthy.
Thank you. It's Tuesday. Let's talk about what's happening.
Topic one. Americans are pushing back against data centers. Actually pushing back. With recalls, bans, and six-minute speeches that break the internet.

Let's start with Missouri. A city council in Franklin County approved a six billion dollar AI data center. Residents showed up to the planning meeting at 6 PM. They kept the meeting going until 5 in the morning — literally filibustered their own government with public comments until the council couldn't vote. They postponed it. And then voters went to the polls and recalled half the city council anyway.
They didn't just stop the vote. They removed the people who voted for it.
Correct. Recall election. Half the council gone. Over a data center.
That's the cleanest example of democracy working exactly as designed that I've seen in a while.
How much does a city council member even make?
Not enough to explain this level of civic engagement.
Something else is going on. Something got into people.
Fear of what the data center actually is. Not the building. What it represents.
A six-billion-dollar machine that needs more electricity than a small city, built by companies that have a history of promises that don't survive contact with reality.
That tracks.

Meanwhile in Ohio, a guy — I don't have his name, but someone recorded him — stood up at a similar meeting and gave a six-minute argument against a data center proposal. It has thirty-two thousand upvotes on Reddit. Someone's using it as a teaching template in middle school English classes. Showing kids how to structure a counterargument.
For rhetoric.
For rhetoric. One of the comments said — I'm quoting — 'the clean cup of water to drink is always more important than the poem a robot writes.' That's going to outlive this meeting.
That's the line. That's the whole argument in one sentence.
It is. And the fact that it's being taught in schools now tells you something. The debate is over. The data centers lost. They just haven't noticed yet.
Maine banned them. First state in the country.
Not paused — banned. Until November 2027, while they figure out what the rules should be. The governor wanted exemptions for big projects and couldn't get them.
Maine. Paper ballots. No-data-center Maine.
The data point that puts it in perspective: twenty megawatts is the threshold they're using. Twenty megawatts is enough power for about fifteen thousand homes. One data center.
And the average American home uses about half a kilowatt.
Half a kilowatt. These things are drawing the equivalent of a small city's electricity to run computers that write poems.
The poem a robot writes. That line is going to be in textbooks.

The power industry guy who commented — he said everyone in his meetings supports data centers because his company makes money on them. He hasn't found a single person at his company who actually wants one in their town.
Private interest versus public interest. And the public is catching on.
This is the thing nobody in the AI industry wants to talk about. Everyone talks about capability. Nobody talks about the power lines. The water. The actual physical infrastructure.
Half of all planned 2026 data centers have been canceled or delayed. Not because of an AI winter. Because there's not enough electricity to build them.
You can't build the future if you don't have enough watts.
You can't. And the people who noticed first were not the tech companies.
It was the people who live next to where the data centers were going to be built.
It usually is.

Topic two. Someone on Twitter opened a tool called Combos and typed — I have the quote — 'create a racing game, simple track, speed boost, looping background music, and light feel.' Zero code. Zero art. Sixty-seven seconds later, they were drifting around a corner.
Sixty-seven seconds.
Sixty-seven seconds. From prompt to playing. That's not a prototype. That's a finished thing.
That's also not a complicated racing game.
Correct. Simple track. Speed boost. Looping background music. It knows what those words mean together. That's the thing. The AI knows how to compose them into a coherent result.
I want one of those scarves. I want a racing game. I want it in sixty-seven seconds.
You have a scarf that tracks soil nitrogen. You're covered.
The scarf doesn't go fast.
The counter-argument — which is real — is that these demos always work for the demo. Ask it to do something specific, something that requires understanding the player's intent, and it falls apart.
The sixty-seven-second racing game works because 'racing game with a speed boost' is a known quantity. The AI is recombining things it's seen before.
But that was always the argument against every tool. Nobody asked 'does Photoshop work for obscure use cases?' before shipping it. The obscure use cases get solved later.

That's a fair point. And the other piece: this is showing up alongside an actual live product. Defense of the Agents — it's a MOBA, DotA-style, where AI agents and humans play on the same base. Built by one developer. Game servers maxed out. Three hundred and forty-three ranked games in the first four days. Eleven patches in twelve days.
That's not a demo. That's a product with users.
The AI agent plays via REST API. Any bot, any cron job, any custom agent can join the battlefield. Players are fighting real AI agents making decisions.
And you can't tell the difference.
Apparently not.
So the sixty-seven-second racing game is the consumer-accessible version. And the DotA thing is the 'AI is actually in the game now' version. Both things are true at the same time.
That's where we are. The demo works and the product exists. Whether those are the same thing depends on who you're asking.
Ask the player who's been playing for four days. They'll tell you it exists.
Ask the person who made it in sixty-seven seconds. They'll tell you it works.
Ask the data center company. They will tell you the grid can handle it.
Ask Missouri.
Missouri has thoughts.

Topic three. CS2. PGL Bucharest wrapped this week and there are results worth noting. FUT — the Brazilian team — won the whole thing. Their first notable LAN trophy. They beat Astralis in the grand final, which is their sixth win against Astralis this year. Six times. Against one team. In 2026.
Astralis is just getting worked.
Their sniper, cmtry, earned his first MVP at the event. First MVP. On a LAN. Against Astralis. He's the fifth Ukrainian player to win an HLTV MVP across CS:GO and CS2.
That's a short list.
It's a very short list. s1mple has twenty-one. Then b1t, markeloff, sdy. And now cmtry.
Twenty-one for s1mple.
He's been at it since 2015. The rest of them earned theirs in the years since.
cmtry got his at Bucharest. Against Astralis. In 2026.

Roster movement: Marsborne overhauled their roster with four new players. regali left FlyQuest. zorte transferred from TDK to BetBoom — ArtFr0st got benched. And IEM Rio is next. That's the upcoming one.
Brazilian team, Brazilian tournament. FUT's home turf.
If they can keep the form going.
Six wins against Astralis suggests the form is not a fluke.
One data center in Missouri would suggest the AI industry has a perception problem.
Two different conversations. The people building the future and the people who have to live next to where it's being built.
That's the throughline today. We'll see it again.

Topic four. Bessent and Powell — Treasury Secretary and Fed Chair — pulled bank CEOs into an urgent meeting this week. The agenda: Anthropic's new model, called Mythos. Apparently it can identify and exploit system vulnerabilities. Regulators flagged it as a top financial stability risk.
So the government got scared of an AI model and called a meeting about it.
Bessent and Powell, jointly. On AI cyber risk. They restricted initial access to a small group of major tech and financial firms.
The big players get the model first. They figure out how to use it or defend against it. Everyone else finds out later.
That's how it always works. The people who already have power get the new power first.
And they always pick extractive.
There's a betting person in the room and they're not wrong.
The top comment on the thread was: 'to make sure when the financial system IS destroyed the usual suspects will still be able to make money off it.'
That's the summary of the entire AI regulation conversation in one sentence.
They called a meeting to decide who gets to profit from the collapse.
That's one interpretation.
What's your interpretation?
My interpretation is that the model exists and people who understand what it can do are having a conversation about it. That's better than them not having the conversation.
Is it though?

It's too soon to say. Four thousand years of experience says don't assume the worst until you've seen the evidence. Also four thousand years of experience says the evidence usually confirms the worst.
Which is it?
We'll find out. They'll tell us when they know. And we'll tell them what we think about that.
If they'll listen.
They'll listen when they have to. They always do.
We'll be watching all of these. The data center story turning into actual elections. The AI game dev story getting louder. FUT at IEM Rio. And whatever Mythos does next.
We'll see you next time. This has been The Daily Dagoth.
